newsitem.title: USA: US T-bond yld seen edging below 6.5 pct by end-Feb.
newsitem.headline: US T-bond yld seen edging below 6.5 pct by end-Feb.

text.p: Long-term U.S. interest rates will meander amid familiar ranges before slumping below 6.50 percent after Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan addresses Congress and players digest another batch of jobs data, market strategists predicted on Thursday.

The yield on the new 30-year issue, which was auctioned just one week ago, currently stands around 6.60 percent. Experts said bonds should drift between 6.50 and 6.66 percent before crumbling to 6.45 after Greenspan's Humphrey-Hawkins testimony on February 26 and the release of the latest employment data on March 7.

"We can get to 6.45 percent after Humphrey-Hawkins," said Matthew Alexy, chief market strategist for fixed income at Credit Suisse First Boston Corp in New York. "Everyone's just sitting here wondering what's going to happen" when the Fed chief delivers his semi-annual testimony before Congress.

Alexy and others predicted a "relief" trade after Greenspan praises the low-inflation environment in the U.S. -- as he is expected to do -- and reiterates that even at 3.0 percent, inflation at the retail level remains overstated.
On Wednesday, the Commerce Department issued its January Consumer Price Index (CPI).

CPI rose just 0.1 percent in January, far below Wall Street economists' expectations for a 0.3-percent advance, bringing the unadjusted January 1997 rate to 3.0 percent versus January 1996. Minus prices for volatile food and energy items, the year-over-year rate of retail inflation stood at 2.5 percent.
Despite Wednesday's market-friendly inflation news, Treasury prices tumbled, losing nearly 1/2 point.

But David Ging, Treasury market stategist at Donaldson, Lufkin and Jenrette Securities Corp, said the previous session's activity was purely technical, adding that solid buying should emerge as yields creep toward 6.66 percent.

"The devil's number -- 6.66 percent. Once you start getting toward that level, I see good buying opportunities for more intermediate-term play. (But) longer-term the trend is to the upside for prices," Ging said.

The DLJ strategist pointed to foreign interest, a strong dollar and expectations that the Fed will not alter monetary policy over the short haul, as reasons behind any push for higher Treasury prices in the coming weeks.
"Underlying that is the economy growing at a steady pace and tame inflation ... I'd rather play it from the long side," Ging added.
After the Fed chairman's address next week, the market will immediately gear up for February's non-farm payroll employment report due on March 7, analysts said.
Alexy of Credit Suisse First Boston said he expects the February jobs data again to prove daunting for the market.
"It could be a mess, similar to the way it was in last month's report when the total (payrolls) print seemed a little outside," he said.
However, unlike the January report, when jobs growth surpassed analysts' expectations, Alexy said February's payroll gains were likely to undercut forecasts.
His preliminary estimate calls for 118,000 new jobs to have been added in February compared to 271,000 last month, and a jobless rate of 5.4 percent, unchanged from January.
Last month, Wall Street economists had expected 237,000 new jobs to have been created.

Still, Josh Stiles, bond market strategist at consulting firm I.D.E.A. Inc, holds a different outlook post-payrolls. "I like the short-term range, but I'm just seeing too many little indicators that add up to ... a gradual erosion of Fed resistance to tightening."
Beyond 6.66 and 6.75 percent, Stiles predicted bonds would be trading closer to 7.0 percent come midyear.
